summary: IMAP4rev2 lets an email client access and manage messages kept on a server, treating remote mailboxes like local folders. It includes creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, flags, searching and selective fetching, and it supports offline clients that resynchronize later. It does not cover sending mail, which is left to a submission protocol such as the one in RFC 6409.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP4rev2 lets a mail program read and manage messages that remain in mailboxes on a server. It defines how the program selects folders, finds messages, retrieves parts, and learns about changes. Sending mail uses a separate protocol.

subtitle: How a mail client reads, searches and manages messages kept in server mailboxes.

tldr.problem: A mail client needs to browse and manage messages stored on a server, including when it reconnects after working offline. IMAP4rev1 had accumulated extensions and older behaviors that needed revision.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4rev2 uses tagged text commands and server responses over a reliable stream. Clients select a mailbox, then search for messages, fetch parts, change flags, copy or move messages, and track changes using sequence numbers and UIDs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9051 obsoletes RFC 3501 and incorporates many previously separate IMAP extensions into the base specification. It does not define how to send or submit mail.

today: RFC 9051 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021 and obsoletes RFC 3501. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 9051.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev2 Does
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol, version 4 revision 2 (IMAP4rev2), lets a client access and manage email messages stored on a server. It treats remote mailboxes as folders that a client can manage, and it supports an offline client resynchronizing with the server.

Clients can create, delete, and rename mailboxes; check for new messages; set flags; search; and fetch message details, text, or selected parts. IMAP4rev2 does not send mail. A separate mail submission protocol, such as the one described in RFC 6409, handles that task.

The protocol assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP. With TCP, the server listens on port 143 for cleartext connections or port 993 for connections that start with TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP4rev2 lets a mail program read and manage messages stored in folders on a server. A client can reconnect and synchronize its view after working offline. A different protocol sends outgoing mail.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
Each client command begins with a tag, a label that lets the client match the server's final result to that command. The server can send untagged data, marked with an asterisk, before it sends the tagged result. The final result is OK for success, NO for failure, or BAD for a protocol or syntax error. A plus sign asks the client to continue a command, such as by sending a message literal.

Commands and responses use lines ending in CRLF. A literal carries a stated number of octets, followed by that many data octets. With a synchronizing literal, the client waits for the server's continuation before sending the data. A non-synchronizing literal does not require that wait, but its size cannot exceed 4096 octets.

A client may pipeline commands by sending another before the earlier command finishes. It must avoid doing so when results could conflict. In particular, a server's message-expunge response can change sequence numbers, so clients must wait before sending a later command that relies on those numbers in the affected cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A client labels each command, and the server uses that label on the final result. The server can also send data or ask the client to continue before the command finishes. A client can send commands without waiting, but it must wait when an earlier result could change what a later command means.

sections.title: Message Numbers, UIDs and Flags
sections.content:
IMAP4rev2 identifies a message by a sequence number or a unique identifier (UID). A sequence number gives the message's current position in the mailbox, ordered by UID. When a message is expunged, later sequence numbers decrease, so a sequence number can refer to a different message later.

A UID is a non-zero, unsigned 32-bit value that increases as messages are added, though values need not be consecutive. The mailbox's UIDVALIDITY value makes stored UIDs usable across sessions: if earlier UIDs no longer persist, the server must provide a larger UIDVALIDITY. Together, mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY, and UID identify one message without changing its contents.

Messages also have flags such as \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted, and \Draft. The server provides attributes such as the message's internal received date, size, parsed envelope, and MIME body structure. Clients can fetch all of a message or selected portions.
sections.plainLanguage:
A sequence number tells where a message currently sits, so it can change when messages are removed. A UID is a non-zero 32-bit identifier that increases as messages are added. A mailbox's UIDVALIDITY value tells a client whether its saved UIDs still apply.

Flags record message states such as read, answered, or marked for deletion. A client can ask for message details or retrieve only chosen parts of the message.

sections.title: The Four Connection States
sections.content:
An IMAP connection moves through four states: Not Authenticated, Authenticated, Selected, and Logout. The server's greeting determines the starting state: an ordinary greeting starts without authentication, a PREAUTH greeting starts authenticated, and a BYE greeting rejects the connection.

In Not Authenticated, the client supplies credentials before most commands are allowed. After authentication, the client is Authenticated and can manage mailboxes. A successful SELECT or EXAMINE opens one mailbox and enters Selected, where message commands are available. Only one mailbox can be selected on a connection at a time.

CLOSE or UNSELECT ends the selection and returns the connection to Authenticated. LOGOUT, a shutdown, or a closed connection leads to Logout. A client should use LOGOUT to end the connection cleanly; the server sends BYE and then the tagged OK result.
sections.plainLanguage: An IMAP connection has four states: Not Authenticated, Authenticated, Selected, and Logout. The client authenticates, selects one mailbox, and then uses commands for its messages. Closing or unselecting the mailbox returns the connection to Authenticated.

sections.title: Mailboxes and Server Updates
sections.content:
IMAP4rev2 mailbox names use Net-Unicode. The case-insensitive name INBOX means the user's primary mailbox; the server determines how other names are interpreted. A server can organize mailboxes into personal, other-users', and shared namespaces. A client needs explicit access rights to use another user's mailbox.

In the Authenticated state, commands create, delete, rename, list, subscribe to, and select mailboxes. NAMESPACE reports the prefixes and hierarchy separators for the namespaces the server exposes. SELECT reports mailbox information, including its message count, flags, UIDNEXT, and UIDVALIDITY.

The server can send unsolicited updates because another agent may add, change, or remove messages. It must report mailbox-size changes observed while processing a command. IDLE lets a client wait for such updates instead of repeatedly polling; the client ends IDLE by sending DONE.
sections.plainLanguage:
Mailbox names use a Unicode format, and INBOX names the user's primary mailbox. Servers can expose personal, shared, and other users' mailboxes, subject to access rights. A client can ask the server to list or manage mailboxes and can receive updates when mailbox contents change.

IDLE lets a client wait for updates instead of repeatedly asking whether anything changed. The client ends that wait by sending DONE.

sections.title: Finding and Changing Messages
sections.content:
In the Selected state, SEARCH finds messages that match criteria such as flags, dates, sender, subject, or text. IMAP4rev2 returns search results in an ESEARCH response, which can report matching identifiers, a count, or the smallest and largest match. FETCH retrieves attributes, message text, or a selected message part; a partial fetch can request a range of octets.

STORE adds, removes, or replaces message flags. COPY places selected messages in another mailbox, while MOVE copies them there and removes them from the source as one action. The server does not create a missing destination mailbox automatically. To delete messages, a client marks them with \Deleted and then uses EXPUNGE; CLOSE also removes marked messages, while UNSELECT does not.

Message sequence numbers can change when expunges occur, so clients must keep their mailbox view synchronized with server updates. UIDs provide a stable way to refer to messages when the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY remains valid.
sections.plainLanguage:
SEARCH finds messages by conditions such as their flags, dates, or text. FETCH retrieves message details or selected parts. STORE changes flags, and COPY or MOVE places messages in another mailbox.

Deletion has two steps: mark messages with Deleted, then expunge them. Expunging can change sequence numbers, so clients must track the server's updates.

sections.title: Authentication and Protected Connections
sections.content:
IMAP traffic, including message content, is exposed to eavesdropping and change unless the connection has protection. The client and server can negotiate TLS immediately on the Implicit TLS port or use STARTTLS to upgrade a cleartext connection. They can also negotiate confidentiality through an authentication exchange or another protection mechanism.

IMAP4rev2 requires implementations to support TLS 1.2 or newer and recommends TLS 1.3. During TLS negotiation, the client must check that the server name matches the identity in its certificate. After STARTTLS succeeds, the client discards cached server capabilities and should request them again.

AUTHENTICATE uses a SASL mechanism to identify the client and may establish another security layer. LOGIN sends a plaintext password and should be a last resort; a client must not use it when the server advertises LOGINDISABLED. A server must provide a configuration that refuses plaintext-password authentication unless the session has protection.
sections.plainLanguage:
Without protection, other people on the network can read or alter IMAP traffic, including messages. TLS protects the connection, and the client checks that the server's certificate matches the server name. IMAP4rev2 requires TLS 1.2 or newer and recommends TLS 1.3.

AUTHENTICATE uses a supported login method. LOGIN sends a plaintext password, so clients must not use it when the server says it is disabled.

sections.title: What Changed from IMAP4rev1
sections.content:
RFC 9051 obsoletes IMAP4rev1, specified in RFC 3501. Appendix E lists the changes. The revision brings previously separate extensions, including IDLE, MOVE, ESEARCH, ENABLE, NAMESPACE, and UNSELECT, into the base specification.

The revision allows UTF-8 in mailbox names and message headers, requires SEARCH to return ESEARCH, and deprecates older response and command forms such as SEARCH responses, CHECK, and LSUB. It also updates TLS guidance and changes how clients handle certain unsolicited responses. Appendix F recommends QRESYNC, CONDSTORE, and OBJECTID as additional extensions, but does not make them part of the required base protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 9051 replaces RFC 3501 and brings many earlier extensions into the main IMAP specification. It updates text handling, search responses, and security guidance, and retires some older commands and responses. It recommends other extensions for more efficient mailbox updates, but does not require them.
